title: Parallel Loop Transformer for Efficient Test-Time Computation Scaling
relevance_reason: Looped transformer architecture designed to remove the O(L) latency and KV-cache growth of sequential loops.
one_sentence: PLT shifts each loop's states by one token so loop l of token i runs concurrently with loop l+1 of token i-1, shares the first loop's KV cache, and adds gated sliding-window attention, matching looped accuracy at near-vanilla decode latency.
key_contributions: Cross-Loop Parallelism: one-token right-shift between loops removes same-position cross-loop dependency so L loops decode in one batched forward pass (memory-bound regime).
First-loop KV sharing plus head-wise gated sliding-window attention (w=64) in non-first loops: KV cache O(nd + (L-1)wd) instead of O(Lnd).
Wall-clock decode latency measured on one GPU (H800 for ablations) with FP8 attention and W4A8 linear quantization across batch sizes 4-64.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: 150B tokens (680M/13B ablation); 1T tokens (1.7B/40B vs 2.5B/60B); 400B tokens (open-source); 100B tokens (OLMo2 ablation)
setup.loops_test: same as training (2 or 3)
setup.baselines: Vanilla Seed-MoE/OLMo with same activated parameters; vanilla looped transformer with same loop count; deeper vanilla MoE (2.5B/60B) for iso-accuracy latency comparison
setup.benchmarks: MMLU, CEval, MMLU-Pro, AGIEval, BBH, DROP, GSM8K, HumanEval, MBPP, TriviaQA, MATH; HellaSwag, ARC, PIQA, Winogrande, CommonsenseQA (open-source)

claims.claim: Sequential looping roughly doubles decode latency and KV memory at L=2; CLP keeps accuracy and cuts latency 37% vs naive loop at bs=4.
claims.regime: iso_param, iso_data (same activated params, same 150B tokens)
claims.evidence_quote: Adding CLP at the same loop count (row (3)) keeps the accuracy nearly unchanged (39.7→39.6, −0.1), while it cuts latency from 9.4 ms to 5.9 ms (−37%) by parallelizing loop computation.

claims.claim: Sharing the first loop's KV cache halves KV memory but costs 3.4 average points; gated SWA recovers it with 1.4% extra KV.
claims.evidence_quote: Adding G-SWA (row (5)) restores per-loop specificity using a local window, raising accuracy from 36.2 to 39.7 (+3.5) while adding only 1.4% KV-cache overhead (280M→284M) and nearly no latency penalty (4.8→4.9 ms).

claims.claim: PLT-2 latency advantage over naive looping holds across batch sizes; overhead vs vanilla grows modestly at large batch as decoding becomes less memory-bound.
claims.evidence_quote: Overall, PLT -2 reduces latency by 47% compared to naive looping across batch sizes and remains within 4–6% of vanilla for practical serving (bs ≥ 32).

claims.claim: At matched accuracy, a shallower PLT-2 (1.7B/40B) beats a deeper vanilla MoE (2.5B/60B) by 0.5 avg points with about 30% lower latency and two-thirds the KV cache.
claims.regime: iso_data (both 1T tokens); fewer params for PLT
claims.evidence_quote: The 1.7B/40B MoE model with P LT and two loops delivers about 30% lower latency than the vanilla 2.5B/60B MoE model.

claims.claim: The latency advantage relies on decoding being memory-bound; extra loop FLOPs are hidden, not removed.
claims.evidence_quote: Compared with a standard non-loop decoder, it adds FLOPs that improve accuracy, yet the latency increase is negligible because decoding is memory-bound [44].

limitations: Latency gains depend on memory-bound decoding; at bs=64 CLP alone is 1.50x vanilla. Compute per token stays LC. KV sharing alone loses 3.4 points. Many in-house details withheld; GPU model only stated (H800) for the ablation; prefill latency not analyzed in main text.
survey_notes: Anchor paper for latency bottleneck (b) and KV-growth (a). Clean ablation: vanilla vs loop-2 vs +CLP vs +KV share vs +G-SWA at iso-activated-params and iso-data, wall-clock per-token decode latency with FP8/W4A8 on one GPU. The speedup is wall-clock, but it is a throughput-for-latency trade: PLT still does LC FLOPs per token, so its advantage shrinks as batch grows (CLP 1.23x at bs=4 to 1.50x at bs=64 vs vanilla). CLP changes the model (loop l of token i sees shifted loop l-1 states of token i-1), so it requires training from scratch; it cannot be applied to Huginn/Ouro checkpoints. Contrasts with the training-free self-speculative approaches (LoopSpec 2609.17184, WaveFront 2609.23033, DAS 2609.34538) that keep exact outputs. Agrees with MELT/LPT/LLA that per-loop KV is the main memory problem; KV-share-only losing 3.4 points is evidence that naive cross-loop KV sharing hurts quality without a local-attention or gating fix.

title: Efficient Parallel Samplers for Recurrent-Depth Models and Their Connection to Diffusion Language Models
relevance_reason: Training-free parallel decoding algorithm for a pretrained recurrent-depth LM (Huginn-0125).
one_sentence: A diffusion-forcing sampler for Huginn-0125 decodes a draft token every recurrence step and refines a wavefront of unfinished positions in parallel, freezing converged ones, giving 4.4-4.8x tokens/s at batch size 1 with about 1-2 point accuracy changes.
key_contributions: Diagonal/wavefront sampler: each forward pass runs r' inner recurrences on all unfrozen positions and appends a new position; positions freeze when relative latent change < epsilon, with max wavefront size bounding memory.
Shows Huginn-0125 tolerates sharing the KV cache across recurrences (keep only latest recurrence's KV), giving r-times less KV memory at matched GSM8K accuracy.
Theory: under equal runtime, diffusion-forcing decoding has equal depth and strictly greater width than AR decoding when wavefront <= hardware parallelism threshold.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: No pretraining; uses Huginn trained on 800B tokens; one-epoch MetaMath finetune for one variant
setup.loops_train: Huginn randomized unrolling (Poisson-lognormal); not trained here
setup.loops_test: Baseline static AR r=32 (also 4, 8, 64); sampler r'=2 or 4 inner recurrences, exit threshold 0.03, max wavefront 128
setup.baselines: Static AR at r=4/8/32/64, adaptive-compute AR (Huginn exit criterion), tuned self-speculative decoding (4 draft tokens, 4 draft steps)
setup.benchmarks: GSM8K, MATH500, HumanEval, MBPP, Minerva Math

claims.claim: Diffusion-forcing sampler gives about 4.4-4.8x tokens/s over static AR r=32 at batch size 1 with small accuracy changes (GSM8K +0.31, HumanEval -2.44).
claims.regime: same checkpoint, same backend, wall-clock tokens/s (not_applicable for architecture regimes)
claims.evidence_quote: We find that on all benchmarks, executing the parallelized sampler leads to significant speedups of around 5x, with only minor trade-offs in generation quality of around 1%, depending on the task

claims.claim: The sampler does not reduce FLOPs; speedup comes from exploiting GPU parallelism in memory-bound decoding (FLOPs are actually higher than AR per token).
claims.evidence_quote: While this approach does not reduce FLOPs, it effectively exploits modern GPU architectures by unlocking additional opportunities for parallelization.

claims.claim: Huginn-0125 supports cross-recurrence KV sharing (cache of latest recurrence only) matching baseline GSM8K accuracy with r-times less KV memory.
claims.evidence_quote: As shown in Figure 3, the trained Huginn-0125 model inherently supports KV cache sharing, allowing us to store only the KV state of the most recent recurrence for each token position

claims.claim: Diffusion sampler beats tuned self-speculative decoding (which itself is about 1.9x over static AR on GSM8K).
claims.evidence_quote: Show that diffusion forcing sampling outperforms even well-tuned speculative decoding baselines for the same model with speed gains that can be smoothly traded off against accuracy.

claims.claim: Requirements for the sampler: input injection and intermediate states decodable to approximately correct outputs; models trained with a fixed recurrence count may fail.
claims.evidence_quote: While this property is generally satisfied, it may fail in models trained exclusively with a fixed number of recurrences r, where decoding from earlier steps can yield nonsensical outputs

Requires input injection and robust intermediate decodability; HF transformers backend without further inference optimizations. survey_notes: Anchor for latency bottleneck (b), training-free. Speedup is wall-clock tokens/s at batch size 1 on A100-40GB in HF transformers (no vLLM), so absolute numbers are against an unoptimized AR baseline; gains at large batch are not measured. It is an approximate sampler (outputs differ from AR; HumanEval -2.44), unlike lossless speculative methods (LoopSpec 2609.17184, WaveFront 2609.23033). Same core idea as PLT's cross-loop parallelism and WaveFront decoding (diagonal scheduling of (token, loop) pairs), but applied post hoc to Huginn without retraining. Also an independent confirmation (Fig. 3) that Huginn's KV can be shared across recurrences, consistent with LPT/MELT/LLA. Note the code URL is split across a line break in the PDF text.

title: The Surprising Effectiveness of Shared Memory in Looped Transformers
relevance_reason: Pretrains looped LMs where later recursions read the first recursion's KV cache plus a short own window; quality-memory frontier at 150M-1B.
one_sentence: Training looped LMs so later recursions attend (one softmax) to the first recursion's full KV cache plus a 64-token own window cuts KV memory 2.0-4.7x vs a matched looped baseline and improves perplexity, with the shared cache acting as a gradient highway.
key_contributions: Memory Sharing recipe (LPT) and its Gated-DeltaNet hybrid (H-LPT): KV size L[T+(R-1)w] vs LRT for vanilla looped, trained from scratch.
At iso-param, iso-data, matched recursion count, LPT beats full-cache LT in perplexity and accuracy; LT stops improving after 3 recursions, LPT improves through 5.
Measured H100 decode capacity and throughput (bf16, 4,096 context, CUDA graphs): memory savings become 2.0-4.8x larger max batch vs LT, but per-step latency still grows with recursions.

limitations: Not compute-optimal (4.3-4.8x decode FLOPs of STD at R=5); fixed recursion count for all tokens; no decode-FLOP-matched dense baseline; up to 1B on one corpus at 4,096 context, no long-context tasks; speed measurements from a research implementation, not a serving engine.
survey_notes: Anchor for KV-growth (a). Strongest controlled evidence (iso-param, iso-data, matched recursions, 3 extra seeds at S) that trained cross-loop KV sharing is not merely free but improves quality. Contradicts PLT (2510.24824), where KV-share alone cost 3.4 avg points; the difference is LPT reads shared and local in one softmax with sequential recursions, and directly beats PLT at comparable cache. Also contrasts with the claim that cache reuse works because keys are similar across recursions (Bae et al. 2025): LPT shared/local keys form distinct clusters. Wall-clock reporting is honest: memory sharing saves capacity, not per-step time (LPT 3-8% slower than LT at equal batch; looped decode at bs=1 is 2.3-5.7x STD). So 'iso-memory' gains translate to throughput only when batch is memory-limited. Notes LT instability beyond 3 recursions with Ouro normalization and nine-recursion instability, consistent with Ouro loss spikes at 8.

title: FlashLoop: Fast and Memory-Efficient Looped Transformers via Lazy Updates
relevance_reason: Training-free inference framework for pretrained looped LMs (Ouro, Huginn) exploiting cross-loop redundancy to cut compute and KV memory.
one_sentence: FlashLoop observes that cross-loop updates concentrate on few tokens and few attention columns and that adjacent-loop KV residuals quantize well, and combines token-sparse updates, loop-aware sparse attention and INT4 KV-residual quantization for 1.52-1.64x end-to-end speedup and 5.2-6.1x KV reduction.
key_contributions: Characterizes three cross-loop redundancies in Ouro and Huginn: nested sparse token updates, stable sparse attention columns, small adjacent-loop KV residuals.

Training-free: token-sparse loops (inactive tokens reuse previous-loop KV), top-K column recomputation with cached global probability mass, INT4 group-wise base+residual KV quantization; fused GPU kernels.
Measured end-to-end wall-clock and peak KV memory on A100-SXM4-40GB; beats H2O and Ouro last-step KV reuse at -75% KV.

setup.loops_test: Ouro 4 loops (dense loops 1-2, token retention 25% loop 3, 10% loop 4 for Ouro-1.4B); Huginn 32 loops
setup.baselines: Original model dense inference; H2O (25% tokens); Last-step KV reuse (Ouro); per-loop KIVI4 quantization
setup.benchmarks: MATH-500, GSM8K, ARC-Challenge, HellaSwag, WinoGrande; WikiText-2 perplexity and Needle-in-a-Haystack at 8K-32K

survey_notes: Covers bottlenecks (a) KV growth, (d) quantization (KV residual INT4 across loops) and (e) kernels (fused update+quant into attention). Its observation that adjacent-loop KV residuals shrink with depth is consistent with WISE (2609.27373, attention routing stabilizes early) and with the convergence-based freezing in the diffusion-forcing sampler (2510.14961). MATH-500 drop of 3.4 points on Ouro-2.6B-Thinking shows reasoning-heavy models are less tolerant; average deltas hide this.

title: Shallow Queries, Mature Values: Depth-Asynchronous Self-Speculation
relevance_reason: Training-free lossless self-speculative decoding for recurrent-depth LMs (Huginn, Raven) using full-depth prefix K/V in shallow drafts.
one_sentence: DAS lets shallow-depth drafts read full-depth K/V of the verified prefix (values mature later than queries/keys), and DAS-Wave combines this with carried parallel refinement and an independent full-depth verifier for 4.00-6.96x batch-1 throughput over full-depth AR.
key_contributions: Measures channel-wise maturation: at recurrence 1, Q/K/V cosine to final depth is 0.79/0.84/0.57 on Huginn; swapping in full-depth prefix V raises draft-target agreement 47.22% -> 66.93%.

Mature-V / Mature-Spec: sequential self-speculation reading deep prefix K/V; DAS-Wave: diffusion-forcing-style carried parallel refinement plus separate full-depth verification (greedy output preserved).
Benchmarks against Lookahead, PLD, Token Recycling, SAM-Decoding, and sequential self-speculation across four R=32 checkpoints with 95% CIs.

Important nuance for the survey: generic training-free speculative baselines (Token Recycling 2.81x) beat plain looped self-speculation (1.70x) on Huginn/GSM8K, so early-loop drafting alone is not automatically the best accelerator; the win comes from combining diffusion-forcing-style parallel refinement (2510.14961) with mature prefix K/V and a verifier. Contrast with 2510.14961, which reports ~4.4-4.8x but is approximate (no verifier); DAS-Wave is comparable in magnitude and exact. Also relevant to KV: DAS needs only full-depth prefix K/V, i.e., it reads a single (final-depth) cache like Huginn's KV-sharing. Agreement 47% at depth 1 on Huginn vs 84% on Raven-Llama shows retrofitted models produce better early drafts.

title: LoopCD: Loop-wise Contrastive Decoding for Improving Reasoning in Looped Language Models
relevance_reason: Training-free contrastive decoding that uses early-loop logits of looped LMs (Huginn, Ouro) as the amateur distribution.
one_sentence: LoopCD scores tokens by log p(final loop) minus 0.2-0.3 x log p(early loop), correcting 'hard' tokens whose confidence peaks early then drops, raising Huginn and Ouro reasoning accuracy by about 1-7 points at 0.98-0.99x throughput.
key_contributions: Identifies loop instability: about 10-15% of reasoning tokens are 'hard' with non-monotonic logit margin across loops, and replacing them hurts accuracy more than replacing easy tokens.
Loop-wise contrastive decoding reusing hidden states already computed, with adaptive plausibility constraint; amateur loop at roughly 15-30% of recurrence depth.
Compatible with early exit (Huginn: 1.94x throughput with gains retained) and compares against MTI, Self-Eval, NoiseCD.

title: Depth-adaptive Inference of Looped Language Models via Continuous Depth Batching
relevance_reason: First end-to-end serving system for per-token adaptive-depth looped LMs (Ouro 1.4B, Huginn 3.5B) with batching between loop steps.
one_sentence: CDB schedules prefill, prelude, recurrent-core and coda as separate queues, refills batch slots freed by exiting tokens, uses a one-step lookahead exit gate for asynchronous batch prep, and realizes 83-99% of the prefill-corrected maximum early-exit speedup on one H100.
key_contributions: End-to-end continuous depth batching (refill and no-refill modes) with depth-aware KV layouts (last-exited copy, single shared slot) and CUDA-graph, asynchronous scheduling with a lookahead gate.

Derives a FLOP-based decode speedup bound and a prefill-corrected end-to-end bound, plus a recurrent-step latency model t = delta + gamma*Nb + alpha*Nc explaining when refill helps (memory-bound regime).
Shows boundary-stage cost (non-looped prelude/coda) limits adaptive-depth speedup: fully looped Ouro benefits from refill, Huginn (2-4-2) prefers no-refill.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: No model training; lookahead and pre-loop exit gates distilled on Nemotron-Post-Training-Dataset-v2 for Ouro
setup.loops_test: Ouro up to 4 (rmin=2); Huginn up to 16 with convergence criterion
setup.baselines: Standard token-level continuous batching at full depth (same codebase; built on HF Transformers, vLLM, SGLang components)
setup.benchmarks: Offline throughput and online serving on Alpaca, ShareGPT, ArXiv-Summarization workloads; GSM8K accuracy for KV-layout and gate ablations

claims.claim: Refill CDB achieves 1.32-1.53x throughput over full-depth continuous batching on Ouro (96-99% of the bound); on Huginn no-refill reaches 1.30-1.37x (83-96%).
claims.regime: same checkpoint, wall-clock throughput, single H100
claims.evidence_quote: At the selected thresholds, refill achieves 1.32 to 1.53× the throughput of CB on Ouro and realizes 96 to 99% of Se2e , nearly matching the estimated maximum for each setting.

claims.claim: FLOP savings from early exit do not automatically reduce wall-clock; in the memory-bound regime shrinking the batch saves little time, which is why refill is needed.
claims.evidence_quote: We find that early exits reduce recurrent-core FLOPs, but fewer FLOPs do not always reduce wall-clock time, especially in the memory bound regime.

claims.claim: Decode-FLOP speedup estimates overestimate end-to-end gains because prefill (3.7-36% of GPU time) is unaffected by early exit.
claims.evidence_quote: Decode FLOPs alone (Sdec ) overestimate end-to-end speedup because depth-adaptive decoding does not reduce prefill latency.

claims.claim: Non-looped boundary layers (prelude/coda, embedding, LM head) slow and complicate adaptive-depth scheduling; fully looped architectures are best suited.
claims.evidence_quote: show that fully looped architectures are best suited to depth-adaptive inference, as large non-looped layers outside the recurrent core (e.g., token embedding, LM head, and unshared transformer blocks) slow down and complicate scheduling.

claims.claim: Zero-shot single-slot KV sharing collapses Ouro-1.4B on GSM8K (0.23%) but slightly improves Huginn (32.52% vs 30.93%), contradicting Ouro's reported near-lossless sharing.
claims.evidence_quote: The results in Table 4 show that the Huginn model is insensitive to the KV sharing layout, while Ouro loses accuracy under both layouts, from about 6 points under first-then-shared to a complete collapse under single-slot sharing.

claims.claim: Depth-adaptive decoding Pareto-dominates fixed-depth truncation in accuracy vs mean depth; a lookahead gate predicting exit one step early costs no accuracy, but a pre-loop gate fails.
claims.evidence_quote: Depth-adaptive decoding Pareto-dominates fixed depth, reaching higher accuracy at every mean recurrent depth.

numbers.what: CDB overhead at full depth (no exits) vs CB
numbers.quote: Even with its staged forward pass and additional scheduler interactions, our implementation retains 95 to 99% of CB throughput, showing that the additional scheduling introduces little overhead.
On Huginn, no-refill performs best, reaching 1.30 to 1.37× CB and 83 to 96% of Se2e .
Across workloads, prefill accounts for 3.7–36% of GPU time.

numbers.what: KV layout: Ouro and Huginn slots, KiB/token, GiB@4k, GSM8K accuracy (full, single-slot, first-then-shared)

numbers.quote: KV sharing enables not only much simpler CDB (Section 4.2) but also substantial memory savings: single-slot sharing shrinks the cache 4× for Ouro and 8.5× for Huginn.

numbers.quote: single-slot sharing retains substantially more accuracy than the full depth-indexed cache: 11.45% against 3.71% at depth 6 and 25.25% against 12.43% at depth 9
Ouro performs well down to a mean depth of ≈ 2.5 and Huginn down to ≈ 8.

survey_notes: Anchor for (c) adaptive-depth serving. Key methodological point for the survey: it explicitly separates FLOP-based bounds (Sdec, Se2e) from measured wall-clock throughput, and shows FLOP/mean-depth savings overstate real speedup (prefill and memory-bound decode). Use it to flag adaptive-depth papers that report only average depth or FLOPs. Contradiction: Ouro paper reports near-lossless KV sharing (78.85% GSM8K); CDB measures 0.23% under single-slot sharing including prefill; consistent with MELT (2605.07721) and LPT (2610.02383) statement that Ouro's sharing must be trained. Huginn, trained with randomized depth, tolerates single-slot sharing (agrees with 2510.14961 Fig. 3). Architecture guidance: fully looped (Ouro-style) is better for adaptive serving than prelude/coda designs (Huginn).

title: Quantizing Recursive Reasoning Models
relevance_reason: Quantization of weight-tied recursive reasoners (TRM, EqR) on puzzles; directly addresses error accumulation across recursion steps, but not language models.
one_sentence: Per-tensor 4-bit activation quantization of a TRM injects a coherent bias at each of 336 block reuses, collapsing Sudoku exact accuracy 84.1% -> 0.0%, while per-block MXInt4 activations restore contraction and near-FP accuracy (80.1%).
key_contributions: Frames quantization of a weight-tied recursion as a perturbed transition operator: 8-bit error contracts back toward the FP trajectory, per-tensor 4-bit error drifts coherently.
Shows activation-scaling granularity, not bit-width or int-vs-float, controls the contraction-vs-drift boundary; rules out calibration size, dynamic scales, SmoothQuant and Hadamard rotation.
Sensitivity grows with reuse depth: the EqR equilibrium model (~288 applications) is most sensitive; stochastic breadth and averaging do not remove the bias.

setup.model_sizes: TRM ~7M-parameter two-layer block; EqR released Sudoku-Extreme checkpoint
setup.train_tokens_or_data: Sudoku-Extreme, Maze-Hard, ARC-AGI (released TRM codebase)
setup.loops_train: TRM 16 deep-supervision steps; inner layers applied 336 times per forward pass (Sudoku)
setup.loops_test: EqR depth D16-D64
setup.baselines: FP, Int8, per-tensor Int4/FP4, MXFP4, MXFP6, SmoothQuant, Hadamard rotation, QAT/LSQ, untied matched-capacity control
setup.benchmarks: Sudoku-Extreme, Maze-Hard exact accuracy; ARC-AGI pass@2

claims.claim: 8-bit quantization preserves accuracy in a weight-tied recursion while per-tensor 4-bit causes drift that removes all exact solutions.
claims.evidence_quote: While 8-bit quantization (integer or float) preserves accuracy, moving to a per-tensor 4-bit format causes a systematic bias to accumulate.

claims.claim: Error concentrates in the most-reused recursive layers and scales with reuse depth.
claims.evidence_quote: The displacement concentrates in the most-reused recursive layers (336× per forward pass) and scales directly with reuse depth.

claims.claim: Activation-scaling granularity, not number format, is the control variable; per-block MXInt4 restores near-FP accuracy.
claims.evidence_quote: In this work, we show that this collapse is caused by activation-scaling granularity rather than bit-width or number format.

claims.claim: The deepest (equilibrium) recursion is most sensitive; per-tensor Int4 prevents attractor convergence, per-group scaling recovers it.
claims.evidence_quote: Yet, our per-block rule restores stability and preserves depth scaling (0.01% → 82.3%).

claims.claim: Test-time stochasticity and trajectory averaging cannot remove the systematic quantization bias.
claims.evidence_quote: Both averaging and halt-head selection keep exact accuracy at 0.0%, while the same selector lifts full precision to 95.0%

numbers.what: Sudoku exact accuracy FP vs per-tensor Int4
numbers.quote: The ensuing drift catastrophically degrades exact-solution accuracy on Sudoku from 84.1% to 0.0% (only ∼25% of cells correct).
Consequently, final accuracy matches full precision (Sudoku Int8 = 84.2% vs. FP = 84.1% in Figure 1; Maze Int8 = 83.6% vs. FP = 84.7% in Table 1).
MXInt4 reaches 80.1% (Sudoku, MLP) and 84.7% (Maze, attention), versus MXFP4’s 72.7% and 85.1%, both near full precision.
Quantizing weights alone is comparatively benign: on Sudoku it moves the tied model from 84.1% to 78.5% and the untied model from 69.8% to 68.9%.
exact accuracy climbs monotonically: 0.0% (per-tensor) → 4.6% (per-token) → 14.5% (per-group-32) → 15.0% (per-group-16), with nothing else moving

numbers.what: EqR FP depth scaling and Int4 collapse
numbers.quote: In full precision EqR scales with depth: exact accuracy rises from 86.4% at D16 to 93.0% at D64 as the final-step residual contracts

numbers.what: Cross-step coherence of quantization error direction
numbers.quote: The direction is near-constant across steps (cross-step cosine 0.99 on Sudoku, 0.97 on Maze)

limitations: Puzzle tasks only (TRM, EqR, ARC-AGI); fake quantization, no measured kernel or latency (hardware discussion is motivation only); many results single-seed; HRM-scale and trained stochastic variants untested; Proposition 1 is qualitative.
survey_notes: Bottleneck (d), recursive-reasoning branch. Cleanest mechanistic statement of error accumulation in weight-tied recursion: zero-mean error contracts, biased error accumulates to (I-J)^-1 mu. No wall-clock or memory measurements (fake-quant only). Agrees with LoopQ (2605.16343) and 2609.30820 that looped models need recurrence-aware quantization; also consistent with 2606.26488 (edge compression of recursive reasoners). Contrast: FlashLoop (2609.29812) finds adjacent-loop KV residuals quantize well at INT4 in LMs, i.e., KV-side 4-bit can be fine while activation-side per-tensor 4-bit is catastrophic in TRM; the two are different quantization targets. Untied control with 7x less reuse doubles Int4 cell accuracy, a direct iso-capacity test of reuse amplification.

title: Quantizing Looped Transformers: Feedback Exposure and Calibration Blindness
relevance_reason: Post-training weight quantization of nine looped LM checkpoints (Huginn, Ouro, R-Llama, LoopFormer, Parcae, PonderPythia, Nanbeige); identifies recurrence-specific PTQ failure modes.
one_sentence: INT4 PTQ of looped LMs fails where error enters the recurrent state without an identity path (Huginn's loop-entry adapter) and because step-0 GPTQ Hessians miss later-step directions; accumulating Hessians across recurrence beats one-step GPTQ and RTN on all nine checkpoints.
key_contributions: Feedback exposure: on Huginn, adapter-only per-channel INT4 drops bf16 top-1 agreement to 10.5% while quantizing all 16 core projections keeps 87.9%; corroborated with IIR filter and Mamba controls.
Calibration blindness: one-step GPTQ is worse than RTN on 5/9 checkpoints because step-0 Hessians have tiny rank (Huginn adapter 43 of 10,560 dims).

Trajectory calibration (Hessian accumulated over all recurrence steps) improves every checkpoint and, with Marlin W4A16, gives a measured 1.21x batch-1 latency speedup and 3.80x weight-memory reduction on A100 for Huginn.

setup.baselines: bf16/f32, RTN, one-step GPTQ, AWQ, Hadamard rotation (QuIP#-style)
setup.benchmarks: GSM8K (full 1,319, 8-shot), WikiText-2 perplexity, ARC-C, HellaSwag, LAMBADA

claims.evidence_quote: On 15 fixed prompts, COCONUT agreement rises from 44.8% after the quantized base forward to 61.5% after 8 latent recurrences.

numbers.quote: On a 100-example GSM8K diagnostic, per-channel INT4 on the loop-entry adapter and recurrent core reduces exact match from 34% in bf16 to 0%

numbers.quote: GSM8K confirms the ordering: 79.8% for 4-step calibration, 78.8% for RTN, and 72.6% for one-step (Appendix Table 9).
At 1.3B, it lowers PPL from 27.35 with one-step GPTQ to 20.84, compared with 51.30 for RTN and 19.57 for f32.
The adapter’s step-0 Hessian covers only 43 of 10,560 input dimensions. Accumulating 32 recurrence steps raises this to 335.
On the full GSM8K test set at grouped INT3, exact match rises from 5.84% with one-step GPTQ to 20.70% with full-trajectory calibration.

numbers.quote: The mean ρ is 1.064 for bf16 and 1.145 after per-channel adapter INT4; the INT4 map has ρ > 1 on all 30 prompts, versus 9/30 for bf16.

limitations: Nine checkpoints up to 4.17B; trajectory calibration does not always recover full precision (17-96% gap closed for non-Huginn); rank gain does not predict recovery; mostly simulated quantization, one real-kernel latency measurement at batch 1; weight-only (no KV or activation quantization).
survey_notes: Bottleneck (d), and one of few with a real-kernel wall-clock number (1.21x at bs=1, A100, Marlin W4A16). Main lesson: where quantization error enters the recurrence matters more than bit-width; non-residual loop-entry adapters (Huginn, R-Llama concat adapters) are the vulnerable point, consistent with 2607.16237's 'coherent bias accumulates' in TRM. Calibration must use the full recurrence trajectory (cf. Q-Diffusion timestep calibration). Complements LoopQ (2605.16343), which handles W4A4/W4A8 with loop-dependent scales; this paper is weight-only. Note that per-channel INT8 is near-lossless on Huginn (within 0.01 PPL), matching 2607.16237's finding that 8-bit is safe for recursion.

title: LoopSpec: Pipelined Self-Speculative Decoding for Looped Transformers
relevance_reason: Training-free lossless self-speculative decoding using early recurrent states of Ouro and Raven looped LMs as drafters, implemented in SGLang.
one_sentence: LoopSpec drafts the next token from an early recurrent depth and immediately starts computing it in the same batched call as the verifying branch, adds a gated residual second proposal from a deeper depth, and achieves up to 6.83x lossless batch-1 decode speedup.
key_contributions: Pipelined self-speculation: branches at different recurrent depths advance in one batched call; draft at d1, gated residual fallback at d2, cascade verification preserving the target distribution under greedy and sampling.
Theory: restart probability bounded by TV(p_d2, p_R) independent of d1; with power-law TV decay, closed-form optimal depths (1.26, 8.85) vs empirically best (2, 8) on Raven-Llama-3.2.
SGLang implementation with branch-wise KV management and CUDA graphs; outperforms trained DFlash drafters by up to 1.7x on Ouro thinking models.

Same idea family as PLT's cross-loop parallelism (2510.24824), diffusion-forcing sampler (2510.14961), WaveFront (2609.23033) and DAS (2609.34538). DAS reports sequential self-speculation on Huginn at only 1.70x on GSM8K vs LoopSpec's 5.9-6.8x on Raven models; differences in model (Huginn vs Raven), hardware (L20X vs Blackwell), engine (DAS stack vs SGLang) and the pipelining design make these numbers not directly comparable; flag as a cross-paper inconsistency. Also notes gamma (step reduction) is a proxy that can overstate wall-clock.

title: What Survives When You Compress a Recursive Reasoner for the Edge?
relevance_reason: Compression and quantization study of the Tiny Recursive Model (and HRM) for edge deployment; error compounding across recursive cycles; not language models.
one_sentence: Compressing TRM for microcontroller-class budgets: pruning, distillation and linear attention keep cell accuracy but zero puzzle accuracy; naive per-tensor INT4 breaks MLP-mixing recursion but per-channel calibrated INT4 recovers it; one recursive cycle matches full depth at 6x fewer FLOPs.
key_contributions: Full precision x depth sweep (FP32/FP16/INT8/INT4, H and n_sup) on ARC-AGI-1, Maze-Hard, Sudoku-Extreme with TRM-Attention and TRM-MLP-Mixing (and HRM on Sudoku).
Carry-trajectory fidelity (cosine to FP32 final carry state) as a label-free predictor of quantization collapse and recovery, threshold 0.83 transferring across tasks.
Deployment recipe: flash-streamed 2 KB embedding row removes 99.4 MB table; INT8 per-step latency measured on Snapdragon devices; calibrated INT4 backbone 3.26 MB (weights-only, analytical).

setup.model_sizes: TRM ~5-7M parameters (6.83M ARC, 6.82M Maze, 5.03M Sudoku); HRM on Sudoku
setup.train_tokens_or_data: Released/community TRM checkpoints; QAT 1,000 steps from calibrated INT4
setup.loops_train: ARC default H=3, n_sup=16 (48 refinement steps)
setup.loops_test: Swept H in {1,3} x n_sup 1-16 (ARC); H 1-4 x n_sup 1-10 (Maze, Sudoku)
setup.baselines: FP32 TRM; FP16, INT8 (bitsandbytes per-channel), naive per-tensor INT4, per-channel calibrated INT4, pruning, distillation, linear attention, QAT
setup.benchmarks: ARC-AGI-1 (single-pass), Maze-Hard, Sudoku-Extreme; cell vs puzzle-exact accuracy

claims.claim: Aggressive compression preserves local (cell) prediction but destroys global puzzle-exact reasoning.
claims.evidence_quote: aggressive compression preserves local prediction but destroys global reasoning: pruning, distillation, and linear attention drive puzzle-exact accuracy to zero while cell accuracy holds.

claims.claim: Naive INT4 damage is architectural: MLP-mixing recursion collapses, attention recursion on the same task tolerates it.
claims.evidence_quote: Under naïve INT4, Maze-Hard loses 0.8 pp and ARC-AGI-1 loses 10.1 pp puzzle exact while keeping 89.2% cell accuracy, but Sudoku-Extreme collapses by 68.2 pp

claims.claim: Per-channel calibrated INT4 PTQ recovers near-FP32 accuracy without retraining, while QAT from that checkpoint degrades it.
claims.evidence_quote: naïve INT4 drops Sudoku to 6.4% puzzle exact while calibrated INT4 reaches 74.5%, within 0.1 pp of the 74.6% FP32 baseline on the same subset

claims.claim: Reducing recursion depth to one cycle matches full-depth ARC accuracy at 6x fewer FLOPs (FLOP-based, analytical).
claims.evidence_quote: One recursive cycle reaches full-depth accuracy at 500 GFLOPs (⋆)—a 6× FLOPs reduction attributable to depth: FP32 at the same depth scores 35.75%.

numbers.what: On-device per-step latency FP32 vs INT8 on ARC (Snapdragon via Qualcomm AI Hub)
numbers.quote: on ARC the FP32→INT8 per-step ratio is 40.20→25.69 ms (1.56×).

numbers.what: Calibrated INT4 on official ARC checkpoint
numbers.quote: demonstrated directly on SudokuExtreme and, on the official checkpoint, on ARCAGI-1 (29.4% vs. 29.5% FP32, Table 3; §4.4).

numbers.what: Carry-trajectory fidelity naive vs calibrated INT4
numbers.quote: fidelity rises from 0.35 (naïve, broken) to 0.89 (calibrated, recovered).

numbers.what: Memory: weights-only INT8+flash vs calibrated INT4+flash; streaming peak
numbers.quote: INT8 + flash reaches 6.51 MB and calibrated INT4 + flash 3.26 MB, the latter within the 4 MB microcontroller budget.

numbers.what: Embedding table share of TRM footprint
numbers.quote: The FP32 embedding table (99.4 MB) accounts for 79% of the ∼126 MB baseline.

numbers.what: Inter-channel weight spread, token-mixing vs attention projections
numbers.quote: On the two Sudoku checkpoints the tokenmixing projections reach a 20.7× inter-channel spread, against 11.1× for the worst attention projection.

limitations: TRM family only (HRM on Sudoku only); Sudoku MLP checkpoint is a community reproduction; INT4 never run on device (weights-only estimate); MCU budgets are analytical projections; fidelity needs a full-precision reference; cannot separate recursion effects from tiny-model effects.
survey_notes: Bottleneck (d) for the recursive-reasoning branch; mostly accuracy plus analytical memory, with a few measured on-device FP32/INT8 step latencies (Snapdragon). The 6x saving from fewer recursion cycles is FLOPs, flag as FLOP-only. Agreement with 2607.16237: both find naive per-tensor INT4 catastrophic in TRM's MLP-mixing Sudoku recursion and that finer scaling granularity fixes it; nuance: 2606.26488 fixes weights with per-channel scales, 2607.16237 says the activation quantizer dominates and weight-only 4-bit is comparatively benign (84.1 -> 78.5). Also agrees with 2609.30820 that 8-bit is safe and INT4 needs recurrence-aware treatment. Note the 'depth effect' (H=1 matches H=3 on single-pass ARC) questions whether TRM's full recursion depth is needed in this harness.

title: Memory-Efficient Looped Transformer: Decoupling Compute from Memory in Looped Language Models
relevance_reason: Retrofits Ouro with a single gated KV cache per layer shared across loops plus a per-loop sliding window, making KV memory independent of loop depth.
one_sentence: MELT replaces Ouro's per-loop KV cache with one KV entry per token per layer derived from a gated latent state updated across loops (plus a W=50 per-loop window), fine-tuned from Ouro with chunk-wise training and all-loop distillation, cutting KV memory about 4x at Ouro-level reasoning accuracy.
key_contributions: Gated momentum latent state h_t = z*h_{t-1} + (1-z)*x_t projected to K/V; total cache O(N*L + W*L*T) instead of O(N*L*T).
Chunk-wise training (sequential across chunks, parallel within) and knowledge distillation on all loops to adapt pretrained Ouro-1.4B/2.6B-Thinking in 720 H100-hours on 32K samples.
Measured on one H100 (HF Transformers, 32k generation): KV 23.71 GB -> 5.96 GB, max batch 3 -> 11, but batch-1 decode slower (8.5 vs 13.5 tok/s).

setup.train_tokens_or_data: Fine-tuning on AceReason-1.1-SFT and OpenThoughts3 (32K samples); 720 GPU-hours on 8x H100
setup.loops_test: Fixed (4)
setup.baselines: Ouro-1.4B/2.6B-Thinking (per-loop KV); Qwen3-1.7B, Gemma4-E2B, Qwen3.5-2B, DeepSeek-R1-1.5B; gating variants (mean, EMA, last, scalar gate); untrained cache-sharing (Huginn-style, Ouro last/avg)
setup.benchmarks: AIME24/25/26, AMC23, MATH500, OlympiadBench, GPQA, HLE, MMLU-Redux, HumanEval+

claims.claim: MELT keeps Ouro's reasoning accuracy while reducing KV-cache memory about 4x and peak memory about 2.9x at 32k generation.
claims.regime: same base model with extra SFT/KD (not iso-data); memory measured on H100
claims.evidence_quote: In contrast, MELT decouples reasoning depth from KV growth by maintaining a constant-size latent state instead of appending new KV entries, reducing memory by ∼ 3×.

claims.claim: MELT-1.6B outperforms similarly sized non-looped public models on most reasoning benchmarks at comparable memory.
claims.evidence_quote: Table 1 shows that MELT-1.6B consistently outperforms all non-looped baselines across both mathematical and general reasoning benchmarks, while maintaining a comparable memory footprint.

claims.claim: Untrained cache-sharing methods (Huginn-style reuse, Ouro last/average KV) significantly degrade Ouro on long reasoning.
claims.evidence_quote: directly applying untrained cache-sharing methods to Ouro, including those proposed by Geiping et al. [12] and Zhu et al. [1], significantly degrades performance on long reasoning tasks.

claims.claim: Memory saving trades against batch-1 speed: MELT decodes slower than Ouro at batch 1 but fits a larger batch.
claims.evidence_quote: MELT reduces decode memory and supports a larger batch than Ouro, at the cost of slower batch-1 decoding.

claims.claim: Training with sequential KV dynamics is essential: replacing chunk-wise training with parallel SFT nearly halves capability.
claims.evidence_quote: Further removing chunk-wise training leads to almost complete failure, halving the models capabilities.

numbers.what: Memory: Ouro-1.4B-Thinking vs MELT-1.6B vs Qwen3-1.7B (peak GB, model GB, KV GB, per-token KV MB, max batch) at 32k
Inference efficiency at batch 1 (TTFT s, prefill tok/s, decode tok/s) for MELT-1.6B, Ouro-1.4B-Thinking, Qwen3-1.7B
Fixed-budget accuracy (AIME26) at ~6.5 GB KV; memory at same performance
numbers.quote: At ∼ 6.5 GB KV footprint, MELT improves performance by ∼ 15.5% compared to Ouro.

numbers.value: 90 h on 8x H100 = 720 GPU-hours; sliding window W=50
numbers.quote: In total, training required 90 hours on a node with 8 H100 GPUs (80GB), corresponding to 720 GPU-hours.

numbers.what: Training throughput slowdown of chunk-wise training
numbers.quote: Chunkwise training results in an approximately 10× wall-clock slowdown.

numbers.what: KV memory gap to dense at 32k
numbers.value: Ouro +~20 GB vs Qwen; MELT +~2.5 GB
numbers.quote: for a 32k-token generation, Ouro exceeds Qwen by ∼ 20 GB, while MELT is only ∼ 2.5 GB more expensive.

limitations: Fixed loop count; no GQA; retrofit only (not pretrained with MELT); sequential KV updates make training about 10x slower; batch-1 decode slower than Ouro and much slower than Qwen3 in HF Transformers; comparisons to public dense models are unmatched in training.
survey_notes: Bottleneck (a). Memory numbers are measured (H100, HF Transformers, 32k generation), not analytical. Crucial wall-clock caveat: decode tok/s at batch 1 is 8.5 (MELT) vs 13.5 (Ouro) vs 41.6 (Qwen3-1.7B), so the looped models are 3-5x slower than a dense model of similar size at batch 1 in this stack, and KV compression does not fix latency. Consistent with LPT (2610.02383) and CDB (2608.09444): untrained KV sharing breaks Ouro, trained sharing works; contrasts with Huginn, which tolerates untrained sharing (2510.14961, 2608.09444). Simplest 'Last' variant (final-loop KV only) is close to the gated version, matching LPT's finding that what matters is having a shared memory read path, but MELT uses the last loop while LPT/PLT use the first loop as the shared cache; survey should note this design split. Comparisons to Qwen3/Gemma are unmatched; MELT vs Ouro adds SFT data, so not iso-data.

title: Looped Latent Attention: Cross-Loop KV Compression for Looped Transformers
relevance_reason: Post-training low-rank codec that compresses the loop axis of the KV cache of Ouro and Huginn.
one_sentence: LLA stores per-token per-head low-rank latents of the loop-indexed K/V trajectory (SVD-initialized, distilled with the teacher frozen), beating head-axis MLA, cross-layer sharing, KV quantization and final-loop reuse at matched cache budget on Ouro and Huginn.
key_contributions: Shows the loop axis of the KV cache is low-rank (normalized effective rank ~0.61-0.63, ~60% energy in one direction) while head and layer axes are near full rank; V converges more slowly than K (r_v > r_k).
LLA codec (per-head) and LLA-2D (loop x head), trained only on codec parameters with KL + attention-output matching, plus on-policy refinement for long rollouts.
Measured H200 capacity: Ouro-1.4B max batch 32 -> 768 at 21.3x; honest that the latent-store path is compute-bound (108 vs 748 tok/s peak), so it is a capacity gain, not a speed gain.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: Codec-only training on teacher activations (calibration set); teacher frozen
setup.loops_test: Ouro T=4; Huginn 32
setup.baselines: Uncompressed teacher, final-loop KV reuse, per-loop MLA (head axis), cross-layer sharing (CLA), KV quantization
setup.benchmarks: GSM8K, MC-avg, MMLU, MATH-500, BBH, MMLU-Pro, HumanEval/MBPP, passkey retrieval to 64k

claims.claim: At matched 4x cache budget, compressing the loop axis preserves GSM8K (0.800 vs teacher 0.794) while final-loop reuse collapses to 0.000 and head/layer/precision baselines lose more.
claims.evidence_quote: The zero-parameter final-loop reuse baseline has the same 4× cache budget and no trainable parameters, but collapses GSM8K to 0.000.

claims.claim: The loop axis is the most compressible KV axis, and this transfers to Huginn where an SVD codec is near-lossless to 32x.
claims.evidence_quote: Huginn-3.5B, where an SVD codec remains near-lossless to 32× compression in decoderindependent evaluation.

claims.claim: Memory reduction translates into batch capacity, not decode speed: latent-store path is compute-bound in the current kernel.
claims.evidence_quote: The present systems result is therefore a capacity gain, not a decode-speed claim.

claims.claim: Teacher-forced codec fitting suffers exposure bias in long rollouts; on-policy refinement fixes much of it at 3-5x compression.
claims.evidence_quote: on-policy refinement on student-generated prefixes raises accuracy at 4× compression from 0.43 to 0.66 and reduces no-answer generations when compared to token-level off-policy distillation.

claims.claim: Long-context retrieval bounds usable compression: reliable passkey retrieval >=64k at <=5.33x, 16k at 10.67x, 8k at 14.2x.
claims.evidence_quote: the reliable-retrieval length (longest context with retrieval ≥ 0.9) shrinks steeply as compression rises: ≥64k at ≤ 5.33×, 16k at 10.67×, 8k at 14.2×.

numbers.what: Iso-cache 4x: train-KL / GSM8K / MC-avg / MMLU for final-loop reuse, LLA, MLA-head, CLA, kv_quant
Max batch at 4k context on H200 (Ouro-1.4B; Ouro-2.6B-Thinking)
numbers.quote: At context length 4096 on one H200, the measured maximum batch for Ouro-1.4B rises from 32 to 128 at 4× and 768 at 21.3×; Ouro-2.6B-Thinking rises from 16 to 64 at 4×.

numbers.what: Decode latency of fast path vs teacher; latent-store peak throughput
numbers.quote: A full-memory fast path caches reconstructed K/V and runs at 74.1 versus 63.6 ms/token (1.16× teacher latency), but does not realize the memory reduction.

numbers.what: Absorbed-attention kernel at 262k context (random weights benchmark)
numbers.value: 2.3x faster than reconstruct-then-attend; teacher latency parity at 4x less cache
numbers.quote: this path is 2.3× faster than reconstruct-then-attend at 262k context and matches teacher decode latency with 4× less cache.

numbers.value: normalized effective rank 0.61-0.63; ~60% energy in one direction
numbers.quote: In Ouro-1.4B and Ouro-2.6B-Thinking, the loop axis has normalized effective rank about 0.61 to 0.63, with a single direction carrying roughly 60 percent of the energy.

numbers.what: SVD vs random init held-out KL at 4x
numbers.quote: At 4×, SVD initialization reaches held-out KL 0.105 after the short conversion, while random initialization stays at 0.771 under the same budget
A model with T = 4 loops over D = 24 layers therefore carries the KV cache of a 96-layer decoder while sharing the parameters of a 24-layer one.

limitations: Latent-store decode is compute-bound (108 vs 748 tok/s); fast path saves no memory; absorbed attention limited by decoupled-RoPE fidelity; MATH-500 most sensitive; >10x compression degrades exact retrieval and long-form reasoning; Huginn results decoder-independent (teacher-forced) only.
survey_notes: Bottleneck (a) and (e). Best-documented separation of memory capacity from speed: memory saving exact and measured (H200), decode speed not improved (latent path 7x lower peak tok/s; fast path 1.16x slower). Contradiction to flag: final-loop KV reuse on Ouro collapses GSM8K to 0.000 here (and CDB 2608.09444 reports 0.23% single-slot), whereas FlashLoop (2609.29812, Table 3) reports Ouro last-step KV reuse averaging 68.33 vs 70.11, and the Ouro paper reports near-lossless sharing; CDB attributes this to whether sharing also applies to the prompt/prefill cache. Also contrasts with MELT, which finds a trained 'Last' variant near its best: untrained endpoint reuse fails, trained reuse works. Agrees with FlashLoop that adjacent-loop KV is low-rank/small-residual.

title: LoopQ: Quantization for Recursive Transformers
relevance_reason: Loop-aware W4A4/W4A8 post-training quantization for looped LMs (Ouro, LoopFormer, Parcae).
one_sentence: LoopQ adds loop-dependent activation scales, selectively loop-dependent rotations/transforms, a cross-loop transition adapter and trajectory-aware calibration to a shared quantized backbone, rescuing W4A4 looped LMs where static PTQ (QuaRot, SpinQuant, FlatQuant) collapses.
key_contributions: Identifies three looped-specific PTQ problems: loop-dependent activation distribution shift, error spikes at loop transitions (state reuse), and multiplicative error accumulation (eps_{t+1} <= eps_quant + gamma_t eps_t).

Loop-aware activation scaling, selective loop-aware transformations chosen by a curvature-normalized cross-loop gradient-variance score, low-rank cross-loop transition adapter, trajectory-level distillation; loop-dependent params <0.12% of model.
Evaluated W4A4 and W4A8 on Ouro 1.4B/2.6B, LoopFormer 3x8, Parcae 370M across seven benchmarks against five PTQ baselines.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: Post-training calibration set (no pretraining); calibration <= 5 GPU-hours on RTX 5090
setup.loops_test: Ouro 4 loops; LoopFormer 8; Parcae 8
setup.baselines: BF16, symmetric RTN PTQ, SmoothQuant, QuaRot, SpinQuant, FlatQuant
setup.benchmarks: HellaSwag, WinoGrande, ARC-Challenge, MMLU, LAMBADA (acc and ppl), WikiText-2 ppl

claims.claim: Under W4A4, LoopQ improves mean downstream accuracy by 68.8% (relative) and reduces perplexity by 87.7% vs the strongest static PTQ baseline.
claims.evidence_quote: Experiments across seven benchmarks show that, under W4A4 quantization, LoopQ improves average downstream accuracy by 68.8% and reduces average perplexity by 87.7% compared with the strongest static PTQ baseline.

claims.claim: Looped LMs are more fragile under PTQ than non-looped: naive PTQ drops performance by over 50%, and quantized non-loop LLMs can beat higher-precision LoopLMs at the same parameter budget.
claims.evidence_quote: In our preliminary experiments, directly applying PTQ to LoopLMs leads to performance drops exceeding 50%. Under the same parameter budget, quantized non-loop LLMs can even outperform higher-precision LoopLMs.

claims.claim: Quantization error grows across recursion with spikes at loop transitions, and can be multiplicatively amplified when the loop map has Lipschitz factor above 1.
claims.evidence_quote: Proposition 2 then implies that errors can be multiplicatively amplified across loops rather than merely accumulate linearly.

claims.claim: Long-context prediction (LAMBADA) is most sensitive to cross-loop error accumulation.
claims.evidence_quote: This shows that long-context prediction is especially sensitive to accumulated cross-loop distortion.

numbers.what: Ouro 1.4B W4A4: FlatQuant vs LoopQ (HS, WG, LB, AC, MM, WT2 ppl, OP ppl); BF16 = 0.7159 0.6717 0.6505 0.5256 0.6823 12.03 5.30

numbers.quote: Under W4A8, higher activation precision provides more tolerance, but LoopQ still improves mean downstream accuracy by about 9.8% and reduces average perplexity by about 17.1%.
LoopQ W4A4 reduces memory relative to the BF16 baseline, achieving reductions of 57.1%, 61.7%, 27.3%, and 28.3% on Ouro 1.4B, Ouro 2.6B, LoopFormer 3×8, and Parcae 370M, respectively.
introducing lightweight loop-dependent adaptations that affect less than 5% of transformation parameters, corresponding to less than 0.12% of total model parameters.
All experiment are conducted on a workstation equipped with an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090 GPU with 32GB of memory and an AMD Ryzen 9 9950X CPU.

limitations: Fixed-path decoding with predetermined loops; dynamic inference, long-context generation and hardware-aware deployment open; no latency/throughput measurements; reported gains are relative percentages over collapsed baselines; W4A4 Ouro still loses ~6-14 absolute points vs BF16 on several tasks.
survey_notes: Bottleneck (d). Accuracy plus loaded-memory only; no wall-clock. Flag: headline '68.8%' is a relative improvement over baselines that collapse to near-zero at W4A4, not an absolute recovery; Ouro-1.4B W4A4 MMLU 0.6823 -> 0.5465. Consistent with 2609.30820 (step-0 calibration blind to later loops; trajectory calibration) and 2607.16237 (per-tensor activation scales fail under reuse); LoopQ's loop-dependent activation scales are the language-model analogue of 2607.16237's finer granularity, and its trajectory-aware calibration parallels 2609.30820's Hessian accumulation. The 'non-loop quantized beats higher-precision LoopLM at same parameter budget' claim is preliminary and unquantified in the text; treat as unverified.

title: LASER: Low-Rank Activation SVD for Efficient Recursion
relevance_reason: Training-time activation-memory compression for BPTT through a Tiny Recursive Model on maze pathfinding; weight-tied recursion but not a language model.
one_sentence: LASER stores per-step activations of an unrolled TRM as coefficients on a shared low-rank basis tracked by power iteration with fidelity-triggered resets, cutting BPTT activation memory about 60% (2.85 GB -> 1.14 GB) without significant accuracy loss on 11x11 mazes.
key_contributions: Finds TRM activations across 24 recursive steps lie in an approximately linear low-rank subspace; MLP intermediate (3072-d) compresses to rank 128 while the 512-d hidden state stays near full rank.
Matrix-free power-iteration subspace tracking with expansion and exact-SVD hard reset; memory advantage grows with recursion depth.
Activations are near-Gaussian without outliers; simulated INT8 after projection adds negligible distortion.

setup.model_sizes: TRM with hidden dimension 512, 8 heads, SwiGLU 4x
setup.train_tokens_or_data: 10,000 procedurally generated 11x11 mazes (9,000 train / 1,000 val)
setup.baselines: Uncompressed BPTT baseline
setup.benchmarks: Maze token accuracy and solve rate (5 seeds)

claims.claim: Activation memory for BPTT through 24 recursive steps is reduced about 60% without statistically significant accuracy loss.
claims.evidence_quote: LASER achieves 60% activation memory reduction (2.85 GB → 1.14 GB) with no statistically significant performance

claims.claim: Weight sharing concentrates recursive computation in a low-dimensional linear subspace, but the redundancy is site-specific.
claims.evidence_quote: The 3072-dimensional MLP intermediate activations compress to rank 128—a 92.5% reduction—while the 512-dimensional hidden state and smaller attention sites grow back toward full rank

claims.claim: The memory saving grows approximately linearly with recursion depth because a single basis is shared across steps.
claims.evidence_quote: As recursion depth increases, the one-time basis cost becomes negligible and the memory savings grow approximately linearly with n

numbers.what: Val acc and solve rate: baseline, LASER k=256, k=128

numbers.quote: Simulated INT8 quantization using symmetric scaling introduced negligible distortion (relative MSE < 0.03%)
The primary compression target is mlp 3072, achieving 92.5% compression at k=128 and accounting for 65% of total memory savings.

limitations: Single structured task (11x11 maze, 5-token vocabulary) likely best-case; no comparison to ActNN/checkpointing baselines; very high variance in solve rate across seeds (std ~36%); training-time memory only, wall-clock overhead not reported in main text; LoopLM applicability untested.
venue: Published at Latent & Implicit Thinking Workshop @ ICLR 2026
survey_notes: Bottleneck (e) memory-efficient implementation, training side (BPTT activation memory), not inference. Low-rank structure of recursive activations echoes LLA (2607.15456, low-rank loop-axis KV) and FlashLoop (2609.29812, sparse cross-loop updates), and the near-Gaussian, outlier-free TRM activations contrast with the per-tensor 4-bit collapses reported in 2607.16237 and 2606.26488 (those are 4-bit; LASER only tests INT8). Solve-rate variance (62.34 +- 36.55) makes the 'no significant degradation' claim weak evidence.

title: WaveFront Decoding: Parallelized Self-Speculative Decoding for Looped Language Models
relevance_reason: Training-free self-speculative decoding for looped LMs (Ouro, Huginn) that batches mixed-depth token states in one recurrent-block call.
one_sentence: WFD keeps a diagonal wavefront of positions at different recurrence depths in one batched call, drafting at shallow depth while verifying older positions at full depth, for 2.42x (Ouro-2.6B) and 3.54x (Huginn-3.5B) end-to-end throughput, 4.81x on Huginn with cross-recurrence KV sharing.
key_contributions: Fuses drafting and verification into one continuous pipeline; reaches the infinite-draft-length latency limit of draft-then-verify with finite wavefront width W = ceil(T/Td); bounded rejection cost.
Cost model: latency governed by serial recurrent-block calls, not FLOPs, in memory-bound decoding; identifies recurrence-wise KV traffic (grows with b*W) as the long-context bottleneck.
Combines with cross-recurrence KV sharing (approximate) on Huginn; reports speedup vs user batch size, acceptance rate and context length.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: No training
setup.loops_test: Ouro T=4, Td=1 (W=4); Huginn T=32, Td=4 (W=8)
setup.baselines: Autoregressive decoding; draft-then-verify self-speculation (gamma=8)
setup.benchmarks: Spec-Bench six task categories; GSM8K (8-shot CoT) and MATH-500 for accuracy

claims.claim: WFD gives 2.42x (Ouro-2.6B) and 3.54x (Huginn-3.5B) end-to-end throughput over AR, 1.27x over draft-then-verify, lossless under greedy without KV sharing.
claims.regime: same checkpoint, batch size 1, wall-clock incl. prefill
claims.evidence_quote: Overall, WFD achieves 2.42× speedup over AR on Ouro and 3.54× on Huginn. Relative to DtV, this corresponds to a 1.27× improvement.

claims.claim: Speedup comes from converting serial recurrent calls into batched calls, not from reducing FLOPs.
claims.evidence_quote: Instead, it converts serial applications of R into batched applications. In the decoding regime, R, which consists of a stack of transformer layers, is memory-bandwidth bound.

claims.claim: Cross-recurrence KV sharing raises Huginn WFD speedup to 4.81x (GSM8K) while staying within 0.70 points of AR under the same sharing; Ouro cannot use naive post-hoc sharing.
claims.evidence_quote: Unlike Huginn, Ouro was not trained or validated for cross-recurrence KV sharing, and we found naive post-hoc sharing unable to preserve its baseline accuracy.

claims.claim: Speedups of WFD and draft-then-verify decrease monotonically with user batch size.
claims.evidence_quote: Figure 5 shows this trend; the speedups of both WFD and DtV decrease monotonically with b on both models.

numbers.quote: tasklevel acceptance rates range from 0.78 to 0.97, with overall rates of 0.92 for Ouro and 0.94 for Huginn.

numbers.what: Huginn WFD speedup with KV sharing (GSM8K, MATH-500)
numbers.quote: this raises WFD’s speedup from 2.54× to 4.81× on GSM8K and from 2.73× to 4.46× on MATH-500.
WFD achieves 2.50× and 2.31× speedup over AR on GSM8K and MATH-500, respectively.
On Ouro translation, for example, DtV reaches only 1.06× speedup at α = 0.78, whereas WFD retains 1.92× at α = 0.80.

numbers.value: single RTX A6000, bf16, batch 1, end-to-end throughput incl. prefill
numbers.quote: All experiments were run on a single NVIDIA RTX A6000. The main results use greedy decoding and bf16 precision.

limitations: Single GPU, two public checkpoints; speedup declines with batch size; without KV sharing, KV traffic grows with wavefront width at long context; KV-sharing variant is approximate and only works for Huginn; eager-mode implementation (kernel-launch-dominated on Ouro).
survey_notes: Bottleneck (b) with interaction with (a). Wall-clock throughput including prefill, batch 1, RTX A6000. Key systems insight shared with PLT and diffusion-forcing sampler: diagonal (token, depth) scheduling batches loops of different tokens; WFD adds verification so it stays lossless. Shows the coupling of (a) and (b): without cross-loop KV sharing, mixed-depth batching multiplies KV traffic, so KV sharing is not only a memory fix but a latency enabler. Independent confirmation that Ouro does not tolerate post-hoc KV sharing (agrees with 2608.09444, 2607.15456, 2605.07721) while Huginn does (agrees with 2510.14961). Speedups decline with user batch size, the common caveat for all looped speculative methods (LoopSpec 2609.17184, DAS 2609.34538 report batch 1 only). Cross-paper numbers for Huginn differ: WFD 3.54x (A6000), DAS-Wave 4.00-4.64x (L20X), diffusion sampler ~4.4-4.8x (A100, approximate).

title: Decoding Looped Transformers Better for (Almost) Free
relevance_reason: Training-free contrastive decoding contrasting the final recurrent state with an earlier one, evaluated on Ouro, Huginn, Parcae and Looped-Qwen3.
one_sentence: LoopCD guides the final prediction away from the first recurrent iteration, in logit space (one extra coda+head pass) or hidden space (zero output overhead), improving four looped families at full depth and matching full-depth accuracy at half the loops (analytic FLOP savings 22.5-48.2%).
key_contributions: Two guidance spaces: LoopCD-Logits (z' from z_R and z_1, adaptive strength from top-2 probability margin) and LoopCD-Hidden (combine h_1 and h_R before coda; single output pass).
Gains across Ouro-Thinking (AIME 2024 pass@1 61.88 -> 73.33 on 2.6B), Huginn (HumanEval 22.56 -> 31.71), Parcae, Looped-Qwen3 on math, code and seven multiple-choice benchmarks.

Half-depth + LoopCD matches or beats unguided full depth on the multiple-choice suite; guidance gain tracks the reference's disagreement with the final prediction, making the first iteration the best logit reference.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: No training
setup.loops_test: Full depth (Huginn R=32, Parcae R=8, Ouro 4) and half depth (Huginn R=16, etc.)
setup.baselines: Unguided decoding at same or full recurrent depth (same checkpoint and prompts)
setup.benchmarks: AIME 2024/2025, OlympiadBench, HumanEval(+), MBPP(+), ARC-C/E, SciQ, MMLU, HellaSwag, WinoGrande, PIQA, MMLU-Pro

claims.claim: Contrasting with an earlier recurrent state improves reasoning and code at full depth across four looped families.
claims.evidence_quote: LoopCD-Logits raises Ouro-2.6B-Thinking’s AIME 2024 pass@1 from 61.88% to 73.33%, while LoopCD-Hidden lifts Huginn’s HumanEval pass@1 from 22.56% to 31.71%.

claims.claim: Half the loops plus LoopCD matches or exceeds unguided full depth on the multiple-choice suite; savings are analytic FLOPs, not wall-clock.
claims.regime: same checkpoint, iso-accuracy; FLOP proxy only
claims.evidence_quote: Note that these FLOP counts reflect theoretical arithmetic workload rather than end-to-end wall-clock speedups.

title: Attention Routing Stabilizes Early: Working-Set Inference for Recurrent Language Models
relevance_reason: Training-free reuse of early-discovered block-sparse attention support across later recurrent steps of Huginn and Recurrent-Llama.
one_sentence: In Huginn, attention support and distributions stabilize earlier across recurrence than hidden states; WISE uses full attention for the first 12 of 32 steps, then reuses the discovered block-sparse support with a custom Triton kernel, giving up to 1.76x attention-only speedup at 4K.
key_contributions: Measures a routing-vs-representation timescale separation across recurrent depth (replicated on Recurrent-Llama-T32: 60/60 examples show a positive gap).

WISE: discovery phase (t <= 12) with full attention, union of block-level 95%-mass supports from steps 9-12, then support-only reuse while Q/K/V and within-support weights stay dynamic; finite-time support identification theorem.
Block-sparse Triton kernel on RTX A6000; reports setup-inclusive attention speedups vs native FlashAttention and quality (F1) by context length.

title: StagFormer: Time Staggering Transformer Decoding for RunningLayers In Parallel
relevance_reason: Staggers depth stacks along the sequence axis for parallel decoding; its shared-weights variant is a two-pass looped transformer with cross-attention to the previous pass.
one_sentence: StagFormer lets the upper stack at step i cross-attend only to lower-stack outputs up to step i-1, so stacks can run in parallel during decoding; the shared-weights variant (two passes of one 18-layer stack) closes much of the gap to a 36-layer baseline but triples KV cache.
key_contributions: Time-staggered dependency between depth stacks via cross-attention to previous-token activations, trained to match staggered decoding.
Shared-weights variant (looping one stack twice with separate cross-attention params) and a recurrent-inference approximation; local cross-attention and p>2 stacks.
Latency gains are simulated (two stacks on twice the chips, ignoring inter-chip communication); KV cache grows 50% (separate weights) or 3x (shared weights).

survey_notes: Bottleneck (b) precursor. title: SPEED: Speculative Pipelined Execution for Efficient Decoding
relevance_reason: Early precursor: speculative pipelined decoding that amortizes weight loads across tokens at different depths in a cyclically parameter-shared decoder.
one_sentence: SPEED starts future tokens from early-layer predictions of a cyclically weight-shared T5 decoder so tokens at different depths share one weight load per pipeline stage, recovering most of the latency of a shallow decoder while keeping the accuracy of the deeper shared one.
key_contributions: Speculative pipelined execution: each pipeline stage passes several tokens at different positions through the same shared layer group; invalidation logic and KV-cache rollback keep output identical to non-speculative decoding (greedy).
Training with weighted per-group losses on a shared classifier so early groups give usable predictions.
Argues parameter sharing becomes a latency win only with speculative pipelining (otherwise it saves size but not time).

claims.evidence_quote: achieving close to the same runtime as the shorter decoder network without parameter sharing across all benchmarks other than WMT-ENDE.

title: Boosting Inference Efficiency: Unleashing the Power of Parameter-Shared Pre-trained Language Models
relevance_reason: Fully weight-shared (24 iterations of one layer) GPT-2/BERT; reduces iteration count at inference by enlarging the Euler step size (neural-ODE view).
one_sentence: Treating a parameter-shared pre-norm Transformer as an Euler ODE solver, the authors run fewer iterations with larger per-layer step scales (searched beta in [1,3]) and pretrain with small step size so that iteration count can be cut with less quality loss; wall-clock forward speedups up to 1.92x.
key_contributions: Inference rule h_{t+1} = h_t + beta_t f(h_t) with beta_t > 1 and fewer iterations (sum beta_t ~ T), no extra modules.
Mini-step pretraining (step size 0.1/0.05/0.01) makes shared models more robust to iteration reduction; Euler error bound motivates it.
Extends to partially shared models via piecewise-linear time-dependent parameters; composes with early exit.

title: Nanbeige4.2-3B on Apple Silicon: Fixing Deployment Bugs and Decreasing Looped Transformer Memory Overhead
relevance_reason: Deployment study of a released 2-loop looped LM (Nanbeige4.2-3B) on Apple Silicon; chunked prefill to bound looped attention memory.
one_sentence: Fixes five deployment bugs in the Nanbeige4.2-3B looped checkpoint on Apple MPS and shows that chunked prefill (256-token chunks) bounds the doubled peak attention memory of its 2-pass loop, extending usable context 2.7x on a 32 GiB M2 Max.
key_contributions: Identifies five bugs (e.g., silently zeroed RoPE inv_freq buffer) preventing the released looped checkpoint from running correctly via Hugging Face on MPS.
Chunked prefill for the looped model: max prompt length 4096 -> 11231 tokens, at a throughput cost (22.8-40.9% slower at short prompts).
Agentic evaluation after fixes: up to 30% of MCPMark subset tasks (from 0%).

setup.loops_test: 2 passes

title: A Tilted Bowl Is Not a Slippery Slope: Compressing Looped Models
relevance_reason: Weight quantization of 33 looped models (TRM/HRM, DEQ, Huginn, Ouro, Recurrent-OLMo-2) testing the error-accumulation account; halting-aware 8-bit finishing controller.
one_sentence: Across 33 looped models, a fixed weight-rounding error does not accumulate in loops that settle; it shifts the settled state (a tilted bowl), so collapse depends on error size vs readout tolerance, and a few 8-bit finishing loops recover collapsed models.
key_contributions: Tests the 'error accumulates across loops' account: running compressed models past default depth, none of 22 series widen along outer cycles; accumulation appears only in non-settling loops (deterministic DDIM) and in Ouro.
Push-vs-room law: label-free sensitivity S and one shared room predict which models collapse (R^2 = 0.72, 18 models); fresh zero-mean noise also produces the cliff, so bias is not required.

Finishing steps: a few 8-bit final loops recover collapsed models (median 5% -> 96% of FP accuracy with 16 steps); halting-head stop + 8-bit finishing controller beats fixed depth by up to 15 points under one third of weight traffic (modelled cost).

Directly disputes the error-accumulation account of LoopQ (2605.16343), 2607.16237 (which attributes TRM collapse to accumulating bias) and 2606.26488: for settling loops, rounding error shifts the fixed point once rather than accumulating, and zero-mean noise produces the same cliff. title: Q-DEQ: Discrete Solving and Quantization for Deep Equilibrium Models in Time Series Forecasting under Edge Deployment Coding
relevance_reason: DEQ with a shared iTransformer layer for time-series forecasting; discrete QUBO fixed-point solver and W8A8 re-forward; not a language model.
one_sentence: Q-DEQ casts Anderson-style DEQ update-coefficient selection as a QUBO solved by simulated annealing or a coherent Ising machine, keeps the fixed-point solve in full precision, and applies W8A8 only in a single re-forward pass, matching explicit iTransformer forecasting MSE within -1.16% to +2.90%.
key_contributions: Local quadratic residual model over candidate directions with 8-bit binary coefficient encoding (64 binary variables) solved as QUBO.
Quantization placed after fixed-point solving (W8A8 re-forward) specifically to avoid accumulating quantization error across iterations.
Storage: parameter sharing 1.80-3.82x fewer parameters; with W8A8, 4.3-12.8x smaller static weight storage.

title: CommonKV: Compressing KV Cache with Cross-layer Parameter Sharing
relevance_reason: Cross-layer KV compression for standard (non-looped) LLMs via SVD sharing of adjacent layers' KV projections; no depth recurrence.
one_sentence: CommonKV shares SVD factors of adjacent layers' K/V projection matrices so their latent KV caches become similar and mergeable, with similarity-based budget allocation, for training-free cross-layer KV compression of standard LLMs.
key_contributions: Observation: adjacent-layer hidden states are similar while KV caches are not; sharing projection weights yields mergeable latent caches.
Training-free concatenated SVD across layer groups plus adaptive compression budgets; composes with eviction and quantization.

setup.baselines: MiniCache and other cross-layer and low-rank KV methods
setup.benchmarks: LongBench, RULER

limitations: Not a looped model; listed only as a cross-layer KV-sharing comparison point.
